patterns.property: lecture key never states the popular belief the lecturer names (or, for C, never picks a side)
patterns.evidence: Three of four lectures are myth-busting (A: danger is in the first days; B: worms are not escaping drowning; D: old violins are not better) and C is explicitly undecided. In every item where an option restates the conventional view, that option is a distractor: A-L-3 'To explain why the middle of the season is the riskiest time'; B-L-1 'It's less convincing than the drowning idea.'; B-L-4 'The worms swam up to the top to get air.'; D-L-4 'Most of them picked one of the famous old Italian violins'; D-L-5 'soloists hear differences other players miss'; C-L-6 'To prove that fairness was the true cause of price cards'. A student who has learned 'the lecture overturns the common view' can eliminate 1-2 options per item. Largely construct-typical of the genre, but it is a cross-item regularity: 7/7, never the key.

patterns.property: intent-next key is the sensible / rule-following plan sanctioned by the person in charge; the careless or overruled option is never the key
patterns.evidence: Every intent-next item offers at least one lax/risky/avoidant option and it is never the key: A-D2 'Play without her shin guards' (key 'Ask her mom to bring the shin guards'); A-D4 'Keep the computer room open through lunch' (key 'Shut the room and leave for a meeting'); C-D1 'Stay for the rest of practice' (key 'Meet his father at the front gate'); C-C-1 'Head home and think it over' (key 'Go into Linton's and talk to Kurt'); D-D2 'Climb up to the branch using the woman's ladder' (key 'Get help from the staff who look after the park grounds'). In the 4 of 5 with an authority gradient (captain, teacher, coach, parent) the key is the authority figure's instruction 4/4. Small n (5), but no counter-example.

patterns.property: main-idea: an option naming one narrow episode/detail from the talk is never the key (key is the topic-level option)
patterns.evidence: In the 6 main-idea items whose options differ in scope (A-L-2 and D-L-5 are parallel-frame and excluded), every narrow-detail option is a distractor: A-C-2 'How a classmate hurt her wrist in tug of war'; B-L-2 'What a group counted near the school car park'; C-C-2 'Why the hardware store closes early on Saturdays'; D-C-2 'Loading the year seven pots into the kiln on Thursday'. The over-general/off-talk option is also never the key (A-C-2 'Keeping students safe at school sports events', B-C-4 'How students should choose a project topic', D-C-2 'How the school prepares for its yearly art show': 0/3). Net: the key is always the mid-to-broad option tied to the specific talk. Construct-typical, but fully regular.

Part 1 key is shortest in 0/16 (chance ~4; p~0.01); key is 2nd-longest in 10/16, longest 3/16. All four authors contribute (each 0/4). Margins are often 1-3 characters (A-D1 key 16 vs 14 'They're twins.'; C-D4 29 vs 28; D-D3 'They are in the car.' 20 vs 'They are at home.' 17), and by word count the key ties shortest in several, so it is only usable as a weak 'drop the clearly shortest option' rule. Batch-wide the key is shortest 12/56 (21%, clean); the effect is part-1 only.

patterns.property: sibling items in the same set leak the key (another item's prompt or option text states the thesis or a fact)
patterns.evidence: B-L-1's prompt names the thesis ('the idea that rain gives worms a chance to travel'), which picks B-L-3 key 'The worms were heading for new soil.' and kills B-L-2 'Why worms come up to find food when it rains'. All four D-L-5 options begin 'Blind tests showing that...', which kills D-L-4 'They could see the violins while playing in the concert hall'. D-L-1's prompt 'what a single old violin can sell for' is echoed in D-L-2 key 'a tiny fraction of what an old Italian violin sells for'. A-C-1's prompt 'after she hears about the gloves' signals the safety objection was answered, weakening 'It's still unsafe for the class.' Also, within every lecture the keys paraphrase one another (A-L-1/L-2/L-3 all 'gradual adjustment'), so keys cohere across items while distractors contradict sibling keys.

checked_clean: key is longest option: 14/56 batch (A 3/14, B 4/14, C 3/14, D 4/14); by kind main-idea 1/8, purpose 1/9 - mixed; length-rank distribution 1st/2nd/3rd/4th = 14/20/11/11
key is shortest option: 12/56 batch (part 2 4/16, part 3 8/24); only part 1 is a tell (listed)

key uses a full noun subject where all three distractors use a pronoun: 2 items only (B-L-3 'The worms were...' vs 'They...'; C-L-2 'These clerks were...' vs 'They...') - below n=3 but a visible frame tell; B-D4 key is the only present-tense option ('It looks like' vs 'It was...' x3)
key paraphrases vs echoes the transcript: mixed (paraphrase B-D2 'removed early the next morning', C-D2 'charges student groups less', C-L-3 'fifteen minutes'; verbatim A-C-3, C-L-4, D-L-3)
identical key wording/idea reused across sets: none found beyond the generic 'To show...' frame; no main-idea or attitude key idea repeats across scripts
relationship kind (3 items): key frames vary ('They're cousins.', 'A student and the teacher who read...', 'Two workers at the same store'); no tell
